title: Etale criterion by separable residue degree for analytic fields
statement: Let $F\subseteq H$ be complete fields with compatible nontrivial nonarchimedean real absolute values and $[H:F]<\infty$ [def-weil-field]. Put $A=\{a\in F:|a|\le1\}$ and $B=\{b\in H:|b|\le1\}$ [def-trf-valuation-ring], and $\widetilde F=A/\{a:|a|<1\}$, $\widetilde H=B/\{b:|b|<1\}$. Then $A\to B$ is etale [def-weil-etale-morphism] if and only if $\widetilde H/\widetilde F$ is finite separable [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension] and $[H:F]=[\widetilde H:\widetilde F]$.

source.place: Lemma 2.1.5(ii) and Lemma 2.1.6, printed pp. 9–10; analytic fields are henselian by §2.1, p. 7.

proof.text: Write $k=\widetilde F$, $l=\widetilde H$, $\mathfrak m=\{a\in F:|a|<1\}$ and $\mathfrak n=\{b\in H:|b|<1\}$. The norm inequalities show that $A,B$ are subrings, that for each nonzero element either it or its inverse belongs to the corresponding ring, and that the units are precisely the elements of norm $1$. Thus these are local valuation domains with the displayed maximal ideals, fraction fields $F,H$, and residue fields $k,l$; compatibility gives $\mathfrak n\cap A=\mathfrak m$. Apply the henselianity clause of [lem-trf-separable-valued-completion-factors] with the auxiliary separable extension $E/F=F/F$. Since $F$ is already complete, its metric completion identifies with $F$ by sending a Cauchy sequence to its limit, preserving the norm. Therefore its valuation ring $A$ is henselian.

source.place: §2.1, printed pp. 7--8: analytic fields are henselian; this clause is also used in Proposition 2.2.1, pp. 11--12. Specialize the existing completion lemma to the identity extension.

proof.text: Assume $A\to B$ is etale. Apply [lem-trf-henselian-valuation-etale-local-factors] with $R=A$, $D=B$ and the prime $\mathfrak n$. All local and henselian hypotheses were checked in step 1. Since every element outside $\mathfrak n$ is already a unit, $B_{\mathfrak n}=B$. The cited statement gives $l/k$ finite separable and equality $[H:F]=[l:k]$, using the fraction fields and residue fields just identified. This proves the forward implication.

source.place: Tags 04GH (lemma-finite-over-henselian) and 04GK (lemma-henselian-cat-finite-etale), via the cited valuation-ring specialization; Temkin Lemmas 2.1.5(ii), 2.1.6, pp. 9--10.

proof.text: For the reverse implication, assume $l/k$ finite separable and set $d=[l:k]=[H:F]\ge1$. By [lem-weil-pbc-finite-separable-extension-primitive-element], choose $\alpha\in l$ with $l=k(\alpha)$. The simple-extension power-basis lemma [lem-weil-pbc-simple-algebraic-extension-power-basis] gives a $k$-basis $1,\alpha,\ldots,\alpha^{d-1}$ of $l$. Choose any representative $u\in B$ of $\alpha$. No root-lifting assertion about $u$ is made.

source.place: Tag 030N (lemma-primitive-element), separable moreover clause; Tags 09GN (lemma-degree-minimal-polynomial), 09G1 and 09G7 for the power basis. Agent-written residue-basis proof of Temkin Lemma 2.1.5(ii).

proof.text: For any nonzero tuple $(c_0,\ldots,c_{d-1})\in F^d$, choose $j$ with $|c_j|=M=\max_i|c_i|>0$. Each $c_i/c_j$ belongs to $A$, and its residue lies in $k$; the $j$th residue is $1$. Reduction of $\sum_i(c_i/c_j)u^i$ is the nonzero combination $\sum_i\overline{c_i/c_j}\alpha^i$ of the basis from step 3. The sum belongs to $B$ and has nonzero residue, so its norm is $1$. Multiplicativity now gives $$\left|\sum_{i<d}c_i u^i\right|=\max_{i<d}|c_i|.$$ In particular $1,u,\ldots,u^{d-1}$ are $F$-linearly independent. This proves the norm identity directly; no discreteness, norm-attainment approximation, Nakayama lemma or defect formula is used.

source.place: Agent-written normalized-coefficient argument supplying the residue-degree calculation behind Lemma 2.1.5(ii), printed p. 9.

proof.text: There are $d=[H:F]$ independent powers, so finite-dimensional linear algebra makes them an $F$-basis of $H$. If $b=\sum_{i<d}c_i u^i\in H$, the identity of step 4 says $b\in B$ if and only if every $c_i\in A$ (the zero tuple is immediate). Consequently these powers are an $A$-basis of $B$, and $B=A[u]$. In particular write $u^d=\sum_{i<d}a_i u^i$; since $u^d\in B$, every $a_i\in A$. Put $g(T)=T^d-\sum_{i<d}a_iT^i\in A[T]$. It is monic and $g(u)=0$. Reducing gives a monic degree-$d$ annihilator $\bar g$ of $\alpha$. No polynomial of degree less than $d$ can annihilate $\alpha$, by its power-basis independence. Thus $\bar g$ is its minimal polynomial. Since $l/k$ is separable, this polynomial is coprime to its derivative; evaluating a Bezout identity at $\alpha$ gives $\overline{g\prime}(\alpha)\ne0$. Hence $g\prime(u)$ has nonzero residue in $l$, so is a unit of $B$.

source.place: Agent-written residue-power-basis and coefficient argument for Lemma 2.1.5(ii), printed p. 9; separability is used only for the derivative unit.

proof.text: The evaluation map $A[T]/(g)\to B$, $T\mapsto u$, is an isomorphism: the monic-quotient lemma [lem-weil-pbc-monic-quotient-free] supplies a basis of the source consisting of the first $d$ powers of $T$, and evaluation takes it bijectively to the $A$-basis of step 5. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-standard-etale-monic-derivative] to $g$. Its standard etale algebra $C=A[T][Y]/(g,Yg\prime-1)$ is obtained from $A[T]/(g)$ by inverting $g\prime$. That element is already invertible under the displayed isomorphism, since $g\prime(u)\in B^\times$. Explicit inverse maps send $T$ to $u$, $Y$ to $g\prime(u)^{-1}$, and $u$ to the class of $T$ using $B\cong A[T]/(g)$. Hence $C\cong B$ as $A$-algebras. The cited standard etale criterion proves $A\to B$ etale, completing the reverse implication.

source.place: Tag 00UB (definition-standard-etale), Tag 00UC (lemma-standard-etale), and Euclidean division by a monic polynomial (the cited monic-quotient leaf).

proof_origin.place: Explicit residue-power-basis proof of Lemma 2.1.5(ii) and the etale conclusion of Lemma 2.1.6, pp. 9--10; replaces the ramification-tower proof with the coefficient argument above.
